plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to build and switch on one n8n workflow for a real task at your job, for example a new form response gets added to a spreadsheet and posts a Slack message, and when a run fails you can find the step that broke and fix it.
plan.horizon14: Later: two or three workflows running every day, each replacing one repetitive task you used to do by hand.
plan.horizon28: Later: a workflow with an AI step that drafts or sorts text, with a check in place so a bad result never reaches a colleague.

picture.name: A small assembly line
picture.line: Every workflow is a small assembly line: one bell starts it, each station does exactly one job, and the item moves down the belt from station to station until it is finished.

chapters.title: The bell that starts the line
chapters.covers: Every workflow begins with a trigger, the one event that wakes it up: a time of day, a form being submitted, or an app sending a signal. You set up n8n, build a workflow with a Schedule Trigger, and run it by hand.
chapters.outcome: You can build a workflow that wakes up on a schedule and does one visible thing, like sending yourself a message.
chapters.hook: Every n8n automation, however big, is the same 2 moves you make in this chapter.

chapters.title: Stations and the belt
chapters.covers: Each box in n8n is a node, a station that does one job. Data travels between them as items, small packets of named fields. You chain three nodes and read the output panel to see what each one passes on.
chapters.outcome: You can connect three nodes in a row and read exactly what each station hands to the next.
chapters.hook: A workflow you have to click is just a slower version of you.

chapters.title: Plugging in your work apps
chapters.covers: To use Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack or similar, n8n needs credentials, a saved permission to act as you. You connect one app you use at work and read from it or write to it.
chapters.outcome: You can connect one work app to n8n and make it add a row or send a message.
chapters.hook: You log in once; n8n remembers it for every workflow after that. Here's where that lives.

chapters.title: Passing parts between stations
chapters.covers: An expression, written between double curly braces, pulls a field from an earlier node into a later one. You use the Edit Fields node to rename and tidy data before it reaches an app.
chapters.outcome: You can take a name from step 1 and put it into a message sent in step 3.
chapters.hook: Send 1 message to 50 people and n8n ran that node 50 times. Why that matters.

chapters.title: Sorting items down two belts
chapters.covers: The IF node checks a value and sends items down a true path or a false path. The Filter node drops items you do not want. You build a workflow that treats urgent and normal items differently.
chapters.outcome: You can route items down two different paths based on one field's value.
chapters.hook: Most 'this automation is useless' complaints come from one missing IF node.

chapters.title: When a station jams
chapters.covers: The Executions list shows every run, with the failing node marked in red. You read error messages, re-run with the same data, and set a workflow to retry or alert you on failure.
chapters.outcome: You can find which node failed, read why, and fix it without rebuilding the workflow.
chapters.hook: n8n has hundreds of app nodes. The one node that replaces all of them is here.

chapters.title: Switching the line on for real
chapters.covers: The Active toggle makes a workflow run without you. You pick one real repetitive task from your job, build it end to end, name every node clearly, and check it the next morning.
chapters.outcome: You can turn on one workflow that handles a real task at your job and know where to check that it ran.
chapters.hook: The workflow that worked on Tuesday will fail on Thursday. Here's how you'll know.

hooksFrom.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to build, test and switch on an n8n workflow that runs on a schedule, reads rows from a Google Sheet, uses an IF node to decide what to do with each row, sends the result to Slack or email, and read the executions log to find and fix the step that broke.
hooksFrom.horizon14: Later, around day 14: you could rebuild one repetitive task from your actual job as a workflow and let it run for a week unattended.
hooksFrom.horizon28: Later, around day 28: you could chain 3 or 4 of your work tools together with an HTTP Request node and a webhook, and hand the workflow to a colleague with notes.

picture.name: A conveyor belt
picture.line: An n8n workflow is a conveyor belt: a trigger presses the start button, each node is a station that does one job to every item rolling past, and the output panel is a window onto the belt.

chapters.title: Your first belt: trigger, node, output
chapters.covers: What a workflow is, the editor screen, running a Manual Trigger into an Edit Fields node and reading the output panel on the right.
chapters.outcome: You can build a 2-node workflow, run it, and point to exactly what came out of each node.
chapters.hook: Every n8n automation, however big, is the same 2 moves you make in this chapter.

chapters.title: Start buttons that press themselves
chapters.covers: Triggers: the Schedule Trigger for 'every weekday at 9', the Form Trigger for a simple web form, and what 'Active' actually switches on.
chapters.outcome: You can make a workflow that runs itself at a set time without you opening n8n.
chapters.hook: A workflow you have to click is just a slower version of you.

chapters.title: Plugging in your own apps
chapters.covers: Credentials (saved logins n8n reuses), connecting Google Sheets and Gmail or Slack, and reading rows from a real sheet into the belt.
chapters.outcome: You can connect one app you use at work and pull its data into a workflow.
chapters.hook: You log in once; n8n remembers it for every workflow after that. Here's where that lives.

chapters.title: Items and fields: what's on the belt
chapters.covers: Why one node runs once per row, where the data sits, and expressions ({{ }} brackets) that drop a value from an earlier node into a message.
chapters.outcome: You can write a Slack or email message that fills in a name and a number from the sheet row.
chapters.hook: Send 1 message to 50 people and n8n ran that node 50 times. Why that matters.

chapters.title: Teaching the belt to decide
chapters.covers: The IF node for yes/no splits, the Filter node to drop items, and the Switch node when there are more than 2 routes.
chapters.outcome: You can route each row down a different path based on a value in it.
chapters.hook: Most 'this automation is useless' complaints come from one missing IF node.

chapters.title: When there's no node for your tool
chapters.covers: The HTTP Request node (a direct call to any service's API), where API keys go, and the Webhook Trigger so other tools can start your belt.
chapters.outcome: You can call a service that has no built-in n8n node and use what it sends back.
chapters.hook: n8n has hundreds of app nodes. The one node that replaces all of them is here.

chapters.title: Keeping it running when you're not watching
chapters.covers: The Executions list, reading a red failed node, pinning test data, retry settings on a node, and an Error Trigger that messages you when something breaks.
chapters.outcome: You can open a failed run, find the node that broke and why, fix it, and get told next time.
chapters.hook: The workflow that worked on Tuesday will fail on Thursday. Here's how you'll know.
